props.title: Star 80

sections.content: Star 80 (1983) represents Bob Fosse's haunting final film, a devastating chronicle of Playboy Playmate Dorothy Stratten's murder that pushes the boundaries of the biopic genre. Like Fosse's Lenny (1974), it employs a fragmented narrative structure that builds inevitable dread. Eric Roberts delivers an explosively unhinged performance as Paul Snider, Stratten's obsessive husband-turned-murderer, while Mariel Hemingway captures Stratten's innocence and rising stardom. The film's non-linear approach, jumping between past and future moments, creates a suffocating sense of doom that makes it one of the most disturbing true crime films of the 1980s.

sections.content: The film fits into a crucial 1980s subset of Hollywood films examining the dark underbelly of fame and the entertainment industry. Sunset Boulevard (1950) laid the groundwork, but Star 80 takes the theme to its brutal extreme. Fosse's direction is relentlessly clinical, using harsh lighting and claustrophobic framing to create an atmosphere of impending violence. The film shares DNA with later works like Auto Focus (2002), which similarly explored celebrity destruction through a true crime lens. SUBHEAD: The Impact of Bob Fosse's Final Film

As Fosse's last directorial effort, Star 80 represents the culmination of his fascination with show business's destructive potential, previously explored in All That Jazz (1979). His documentary-style approach, mixing real footage with recreation, would influence later true crime films like I, Tonya (2017). The film's unflinching examination of toxic masculinity and celebrity culture remains disturbingly relevant, presaging later tragedies in the entertainment industry.
